hero.title: A hand built for the complexity of everyday life.
hero.lead: Cook a meal. Fold the laundry. Pick up a tool and use it. Tendra Hand is the first step toward a robot that does everyday work as well as a person, starting with the hardest part: the hand. Built in the open, so anyone can learn from it and build on it.

story.title: Robots that do what we do.
body: Most robots today work in factories, behind fences, doing one job over and over. A home is different. Every kitchen, every drawer and every task is a little new.
The goal is a robot that can cook, clean and use tools as well as a person. Not by following a script, but by understanding the job and carrying it out, step by step.
points: Understands the job, not just the motion

story.title: Everything starts with the hand.
body: Almost everything useful we do goes through our hands. Cracking an egg, turning a key, holding a knife. A simple two-claw gripper can't do any of it well.
So we build the hand first, and we build it like ours: slim fingers pulled by cords called tendons, with the motors further back in the forearm, just like our muscles.
points: Slim fingers, motors in the forearm
Pulled by tendons, like your own

story.title: Every joint, free to move.
body: Your hand can make more than 20 separate motions. Tendra Hand V1 is designed with 20 joints, and almost every one has its own motor, so a fingertip can bend while the rest of the hand stays still.

That freedom is what turns grabbing into skill: a careful pinch, a firm grip, an object rolled between the fingers. Today a thumb and index finger prototype exists, and the full hand moves in simulation.

story.title: Open, down to the last part.
body: Big ideas move faster when everyone can see how they work. Every part of Tendra Hand, from the 3D design to the code to the notes on what went wrong, is shared in public.
Take it apart. Learn how a robot hand works. Borrow an idea for your own project, or build on it. The parts print on an ordinary 3D printer.

story.title: A hand that learns.
body: Building the hand is half the work. The other half is teaching it. A virtual copy of the hand is already practising how to pick things up in simulation, learning by trial and error long before the real one is ready.
Next it gets senses: touch in the fingertips and eyes to see the world. Then AI that understands what you ask, plans the steps and learns from every try.
